lessons.title: Word Detectives: Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.subject: Vocabulary
lessons.learning_intention: We are learning to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words by looking at their parts (prefixes, base words and suffixes) and the words around them.
success_criteria: I can name the prefix, base word and suffix in a word.
I can explain what the prefixes un-, re- and pre- and the suffixes -ful and -less mean.
I can use a context clue in a sentence to work out a new word.
I can use 5 new words correctly in my own sentences.
lessons.prior_knowledge: The child can read common words and knows that words can be made of smaller parts.
lessons.explicit_teaching:
Say: Many long words are really small parts joined together. A base word carries the main meaning. A prefix is a group of letters added to the FRONT of a base word and changes its meaning. A suffix is added to the END.

Prefixes to teach today:
- un- means 'not' (unhappy = not happy)
- re- means 'again' (rebuild = build again)
- pre- means 'before' (preheat = heat before)

Suffixes to teach today:
- -ful means 'full of' (careful = full of care)
- -less means 'without' (careless = without care)

Write each word on a card, then cut or fold the card to split the word into its parts. Show how the base word stays the same while the meaning changes.

Context clues: when we meet a word we do not know, we can read the sentence around it. Look for a word or phrase that means the same thing, the opposite, or an example. Think aloud: 'I did not want to go, I was reluctant to jump. The sentence says I did not want to, so reluctant must mean unwilling.'
lessons.worked_example: Word: unbreakable. Step 1, find the base word: break. Step 2, find the prefix: un- (not). Step 3, find the suffix: -able (able to be). Step 4, put the meanings together: not able to be broken. Now check it in a sentence: 'The unbreakable toy survived the fall.' It makes sense.
lessons.guided_practice: Together, split these words into prefix, base and suffix, and say the meaning aloud: replay, unkind, hopeless, thankful, prepay. Then read this sentence and find the clue: 'The kitten was timid, too shy to come out from under the bed.' Which words help us understand timid?
lessons.independent_task: Part A: Copy and complete a table with 10 words (rebuild, unfair, careful, fearless, preview, unlock, helpful, endless, reread, unsafe). For each, write the prefix or suffix, the base word and the meaning. Part B: Choose 5 of the words and write a sentence for each that shows you understand the meaning. Part C: Find 3 new words in a book you are reading that have a prefix or suffix and add them to your table.
lessons.response_prompt: Write one paragraph explaining how knowing about prefixes and suffixes helps you read a hard word.
lessons.evidence_requirement: A photo or scan of the completed table and the 5 sentences.
lessons.self_check: Did I find the base word first? Does my meaning make sense in the sentence? Did I use a capital letter and full stop in each sentence?
lessons.reflection_prompt: Which word part was the easiest to spot? Which one was tricky and why?
lessons.offline_alternative: Use a printed dictionary and any chapter book from home. All activities can be done with pencil and paper.
lessons.accessibility_notes: Child may dictate sentences to an adult. Use colour to mark prefix, base and suffix. Reduce the table to 6 words if needed.
lessons.source_note: Written for Side Quest. Aligned to NSW English K-10 Stage 2 vocabulary outcome EN2-VOCAB-01. Parent to verify alignment against the NESA syllabus.

quiz.question: What does the prefix 'un-' mean in the word 'unhappy'?
quiz.explanation: The prefix un- means 'not', so unhappy means not happy.

quiz.question: What does the suffix '-less' mean in 'careless'?
quiz.explanation: The suffix -less means 'without', so careless means without care.

quiz.question: 'I felt reluctant to jump, so I stood at the edge, unwilling to move.' What does 'reluctant' mean?
quiz.explanation: The clue 'unwilling to move' gives the meaning of reluctant.

lessons.title: Reading a Narrative: Orientation, Complication, Resolution
lessons.subject: Reading comprehension
lessons.learning_intention: We are learning to read a short story and identify its structure and key details so we can understand what happens and why.
success_criteria: I can name the three main parts of a narrative.
I can say who the characters are and where and when the story happens.
I can explain the problem and how it is solved.
I can answer questions using evidence from the text.
lessons.prior_knowledge: The child can read a short paragraph independently and knows that stories have a beginning, middle and end.
lessons.explicit_teaching:
Say: A narrative is a story. Most stories have three parts.

1. Orientation: tells us WHO the characters are and WHERE and WHEN the story happens.
2. Complication: the problem that the characters must deal with. This is the most exciting part.
3. Resolution: how the problem is solved or ends.

Good readers stop and ask questions as they read: Who is this about? What do they want? What is getting in the way? How does it end?

When we answer a question we go back to the text and find the words that prove our answer. This is called using evidence.

TEXT TO READ: 'Mia's grandfather had lost his old brass key. Mia searched the shed, the garden and the kitchen drawers without any luck. At last she noticed a glint under the hedge where Biscuit the dog had been digging. She pulled out the key, brushed off the mud and hurried back to Grandpa, who gave her a big hug.'
lessons.worked_example: Question: Who is the main character? Answer: Mia. Evidence: the first sentence names Mia and the story follows what she does. Question: What is the problem? Answer: Grandpa has lost his key. Evidence: 'had lost his old brass key'.
lessons.guided_practice: Read the story aloud together. Highlight the orientation in yellow, the complication in pink and the resolution in green. Then discuss: where did Mia look first? What clue helped her find the key?
lessons.independent_task: Read the story again quietly. Draw a 3-box storyboard and label the boxes Orientation, Complication and Resolution. In each box write one or two sentences and draw a quick picture. Then answer in full sentences: (1) Who are the characters? (2) Where did Mia find the key? (3) How do you think Grandpa felt at the end? Copy the words from the text that support your answer.
lessons.response_prompt: Write 3 to 4 sentences retelling the story in your own words, in the right order.
lessons.evidence_requirement: A photo of the storyboard and the written answers.
lessons.self_check: Did I answer in full sentences? Did I include a quote from the text to back up my answer?
lessons.reflection_prompt: Think of a story you know. What was the problem and how was it solved?
lessons.offline_alternative: Read aloud from a picture book at home and use the same three-part storyboard.
lessons.accessibility_notes: Parent can read the text aloud. Child can answer orally and have an adult scribe the answers.
lessons.source_note: Original passage written for Side Quest. Aligned to NSW English K-10 Stage 2 reading outcome EN2-RECOM-01. Parent to verify alignment against the NESA syllabus.

quiz.question: Who is the main character in the story?
quiz.explanation: The story follows Mia as she searches for the key.

quiz.question: What is the problem (complication) in the story?
quiz.explanation: The story begins with Grandpa losing his old brass key.

quiz.question: Where did Mia find the key?
quiz.explanation: Mia saw a glint under the hedge where Biscuit had been digging.

lessons.title: Writing a Narrative with a Clear Structure
lessons.subject: Writing
lessons.learning_intention: We are learning to plan and write a short narrative with an orientation, a complication and a resolution, and to improve it by editing.
success_criteria: I can plan my story using a story mountain.
I can write an orientation that names the characters, setting and time.
I can write a problem and a solution that make sense.
I can use time connectives such as first, then, later and finally.
I can check my writing for capital letters, full stops and spelling.
materials: Story mountain template (draw one on paper)
lessons.prior_knowledge: The child has completed the lesson Reading a Narrative or can already name the parts of a story.
lessons.explicit_teaching:
Say: Writers plan before they write. A story mountain helps us plan. Draw a mountain with five points: 1) Beginning (who, where, when), 2) Build-up (something starts to go wrong), 3) Top of the mountain (the biggest problem), 4) Solving the problem, 5) Ending (how everyone feels).

Show how to turn each point into one paragraph. Teach time connectives: first, next, then, after that, later, suddenly, finally. Show that a new paragraph starts when the time, place or action changes.

Show how to make a sentence stronger: 'The dog ran.' becomes 'The muddy dog raced across the garden.' Add one describing word and one detail about where or how.

Editing: read your writing aloud, then check three things with your coloured pen: capital letters, full stops and spelling.
lessons.worked_example: Plan: Beginning, Kai and his sister camp in the backyard on a summer night. Build-up, they hear a rustling sound. Top, a shape moves outside the tent. Solving, they shine the torch and see a hedgehog. Ending, they laugh and share their snacks. First paragraph: 'On a warm summer night, Kai and his sister Lily set up their tent in the backyard. They had torches, blankets and a bag of marshmallows.'
lessons.guided_practice: Choose a story idea together (a lost pet, a surprise visitor, a broken toy). Fill in the story mountain with one sentence at each point. Say the first paragraph aloud before writing it.
lessons.independent_task: Using your plan, write a story of at least 3 paragraphs (about 120 to 200 words). Use at least 3 different time connectives and at least 2 describing words per paragraph. When finished, read it aloud, then edit with a coloured pen and write a final copy.
lessons.response_prompt: Give your story a title and write one sentence about what you are proudest of in it.
lessons.evidence_requirement: A photo of the story mountain plan and the final written story.
lessons.self_check: Does my story have a beginning, a problem and a solution? Did I use time connectives? Did I check capital letters, full stops and spelling?
lessons.reflection_prompt: What was the hardest part of planning? What would you change if you wrote it again?
lessons.offline_alternative: Entirely pencil and paper. The child may tell the story aloud first and then write it down.
lessons.accessibility_notes: Child can write 2 paragraphs instead of 3, or dictate parts to an adult. Provide a sentence starter list of connectives.
lessons.source_note: Written for Side Quest. Aligned to NSW English K-10 Stage 2 creating written text outcome EN2-CWT-01. Parent to verify alignment against the NESA syllabus.

quiz.question: Which part of a narrative introduces the characters and setting?
quiz.explanation: The orientation tells us who, where and when.

quiz.question: Which sentence starts with a time connective?
options: Later that afternoon, the rain stopped.
quiz.explanation: 'Later that afternoon' tells us when something happens.

quiz.question: What happens in the resolution?
options: The problem is solved or ends
quiz.explanation: The resolution is how the problem is solved.

lessons.title: Spelling: Adding -ing and -ed
lessons.subject: Spelling
lessons.learning_intention: We are learning the spelling rules for adding -ing and -ed to base words, so we can spell them correctly when we write.
success_criteria: I can drop the silent e before adding -ing or -ed.
I can double the last letter in short words that end in one vowel and one consonant.
I can change y to i before -ed when a consonant comes before the y.
I can spell 15 words using these rules.
lessons.prior_knowledge: The child knows vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and can identify consonants.
lessons.explicit_teaching:
Say: -ing and -ed are suffixes. When we add them, the base word sometimes changes. There are four patterns.

Rule 1, drop the e: if a word ends in a silent e, drop the e before adding -ing or -ed. make becomes making, hope becomes hoped.

Rule 2, double the last letter: if a short word (one syllable) ends in ONE vowel followed by ONE consonant, double the last letter. stop becomes stopping and stopped, hop becomes hopping.

Rule 3, nothing changes: if the word ends in two consonants or two vowels before the last letter, just add the suffix. jump becomes jumping, rain becomes raining.

Rule 4, y to i: if a word ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i before -ed (try becomes tried), but keep the y before -ing (trying). If a vowel comes before the y, just add the suffix (play becomes played).
lessons.worked_example: Word: plan. It is short and ends in one vowel plus one consonant, so double the n: planning, planned. Word: smile. It ends in a silent e, so drop the e: smiling, smiled. Word: carry. It ends in consonant plus y: carrying (keep y), carried (change y to i).
lessons.guided_practice: Sort these words into the four rule groups and add -ing: bake, hug, wait, cry, chase, skip, play. Say the rule aloud before writing each answer.
lessons.independent_task: Add -ing and -ed to each of these 15 words and write both forms: hope, jog, clap, bake, rain, try, play, shop, cry, lift, wave, nod, stay, hurry, name. Then write 5 sentences, each using a different word from your list in -ing or -ed form. Finally, ask a parent to read out 5 of the words and spell them without looking.
lessons.response_prompt: Write the four rules in your own words and give one example for each.
lessons.evidence_requirement: A photo of the completed word list and 5 sentences, plus the parent's mark out of 5 for the spelling test.
lessons.self_check: For each word did I check the ending? Did I say which rule I used?
lessons.reflection_prompt: Which rule is easiest to remember? Which one do you need to practise more?
lessons.offline_alternative: Practise on paper or with magnetic letters. A parent can read the spelling words aloud.
lessons.accessibility_notes: Reduce to 10 words and one rule per day over 4 days if needed. Use letter tiles for hands-on practice.
lessons.source_note: Written for Side Quest. Aligned to NSW English K-10 Stage 2 spelling outcome EN2-SPELL-01. Parent to verify alignment against the NESA syllabus.

quiz.question: What is 'make' with -ing added?
quiz.explanation: Drop the silent e before adding -ing.

quiz.question: What is 'stop' with -ed added?
quiz.explanation: Stop is a short word ending in one vowel plus one consonant, so double the p.

quiz.question: What is 'try' with -ed added?
quiz.explanation: Change y to i before -ed when a consonant comes before the y.

lessons.title: Speaking: Give a Two-Minute Talk
lessons.subject: Oral language
lessons.learning_intention: We are learning to plan and give a short talk to a familiar audience, using a clear voice and a clear structure.
success_criteria: I can plan a talk with an opening, three main points and a closing.
I can speak clearly, at a good pace, and loud enough to be heard.
I can look at my audience while I speak.
I can answer one question from the audience.
materials: A topic the child knows well (a pet, a hobby, a favourite place)
Palm cards or small pieces of paper (4)
Optional: device to record the talk
lessons.prior_knowledge: The child can talk about a familiar topic in full sentences.
lessons.explicit_teaching:
Say: A good talk has a clear shape. Opening: say hello and tell the audience what your talk is about, with a hook such as a question or interesting fact. Three main points: one idea per point, each with a detail or example. Closing: sum up in one sentence and say thank you.

Delivery skills:
- Volume: loud enough for the person furthest away to hear.
- Pace: not too fast. Pause at the end of each sentence.
- Eye contact: look up from your cards and glance at your audience.
- Body: stand tall, feet still, hands relaxed.

Palm cards hold key words only, not full sentences. This helps us speak rather than read.
lessons.worked_example: Topic: My dog Biscuit. Opening: 'Did you know dogs can learn over 100 words? Today I will tell you about my dog Biscuit.' Point 1: What Biscuit looks like. Point 2: Tricks Biscuit can do. Point 3: Why I love him. Closing: 'Biscuit is my best friend. Thank you for listening.'
lessons.guided_practice: Pick a topic together and write the key words for each part on four palm cards. Practise the opening aloud three times, with a different volume each time (quiet, medium, clear and strong). Decide which volume works best.
lessons.independent_task: Plan your own two-minute talk on a topic you choose. Write your opening, three points and closing as key words on four palm cards. Practise twice alone, then give the talk to a parent or family member. Ask the audience to give one question at the end and answer it.
lessons.response_prompt: After your talk, write 2 to 3 sentences about what went well and one thing you will do differently next time.
lessons.evidence_requirement: A photo of the palm cards, and either a short recording of the talk or a parent's completed checklist (volume, pace, eye contact, structure).
lessons.self_check: Did I have an opening, three points and a closing? Did I speak clearly and slowly enough? Did I look at my audience?
lessons.reflection_prompt: How did you feel before and after your talk? What helped you feel more confident?
lessons.offline_alternative: Give the talk to family in person with no recording. A parent completes the checklist.
lessons.accessibility_notes: A child who finds speaking hard may start with a one-minute talk, present to one trusted person, or use pictures instead of words on the cards.
lessons.source_note: Written for Side Quest. Aligned to NSW English K-10 Stage 2 oral language outcome EN2-OLC-01. Parent to verify alignment against the NESA syllabus.

quiz.question: What should go on palm cards?
quiz.explanation: Key words remind us what to say without reading the whole talk.

quiz.question: Why is eye contact important?
options: It shows you are speaking to your audience
quiz.explanation: Looking at the audience keeps them interested and connected.

quiz.question: Which is a good opening?
options: Um, I forgot what to say.
Did you know dogs can learn over 100 words? Today I will tell you about my dog.
I do not want to do this.
quiz.explanation: A good opening has a hook and says what the talk is about.

lessons.title: Handwriting: Joining Letters Fluently
lessons.subject: Handwriting
lessons.learning_intention: We are learning to join letters smoothly and consistently so our handwriting is easy to read and quick to write.
success_criteria: I can sit with good posture and hold my pencil correctly.
I can join common letter pairs such as ai, ee, ing, ou and th.
I can keep my letters the same size and sitting on the line.
I can leave an even space between words.
materials: A handwriting model (NSW Foundation Style joined script, from a printed guide or school font chart)
lessons.prior_knowledge: The child can form all lower-case and upper-case letters correctly.
lessons.explicit_teaching:
Say: Joined handwriting helps us write faster and keeps words together. Before we write, check our body. Feet flat on the floor, back straight, paper tilted slightly, pencil held with a light grip.

Most joins start from the baseline (the line the letters sit on) and travel up to the next letter. Letters with ascenders (b, d, h, k, l) go tall. Letters with descenders (g, j, p, q, y) go below the line.

Practise in this order: (1) joins from the baseline, such as ai, ee, ou, an; (2) the ending -ing; (3) the blend th; (4) whole words. Each time, say the letters quietly as you write.

Spacing: leave the width of a finger or a letter 'o' between words.
lessons.worked_example: Write the word 'thing' slowly: t-h joined, then i-n-g joined, with the g's tail dropping below the line. Check: do all letters touch the baseline? Is the g's tail below the line? Are the letters the same height?
lessons.guided_practice: Trace and copy three lines of each pair: ai, ee, ou, an. Then copy these words: rain, green, found, thing. After each line, circle your best joined word with a coloured pencil.
lessons.independent_task: Write the following sentence three times in joined handwriting, focusing on neat letters and even spacing: 'The green frog found a thing in the rain.' Then write 3 sentences of your own about something you did this week, again in joined handwriting.
lessons.response_prompt: Look at your best line. Write one sentence saying what makes it your best.
lessons.evidence_requirement: A photo of the page of handwriting, including the three copied sentences and the three original sentences.
lessons.self_check: Are my letters on the line and the same size? Are my joins smooth? Is my spacing even?
lessons.reflection_prompt: Which letters or joins are still tricky? Plan one thing to practise tomorrow.
lessons.offline_alternative: Practise in a notebook or with a finger in a tray of salt or sand before writing on paper.
lessons.accessibility_notes: Use a pencil grip or thicker pencil if helpful. Reduce to one line per join. A child with fine motor difficulty may practise for shorter periods more often.
lessons.source_note: Written for Side Quest. Aligned to NSW English K-10 Stage 2 handwriting outcome EN2-HANDW-01. Parent to verify alignment against the NESA syllabus and the handwriting style they choose.

quiz.question: Which letter has a descender?
quiz.explanation: The letter g has a tail that goes below the line.

quiz.question: How wide should the space between words be?
options: About the width of a letter o or a finger
As wide as a whole line
quiz.explanation: Even spacing makes writing easier to read.

quiz.question: Where do most letter joins start?
options: At the top of the line
In the middle of the page
quiz.explanation: Most joins start on the baseline and flow up to the next letter.
